reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A group of genetically heterogeneous myopathies unified by a common histological picture of myofibrillar disintegration with abnormal protein aggregates
Weakness is frequently distal or mixed distal and proximal at onset, distinguishing it from most limb-girdle dystrophies
Cardiac involvement, including cardiomyopathy and conduction disease, is common and can dominate the clinical picture, sometimes preceding overt weakness
Caused by mutations in genes for Z-disc and associated proteins, with desmin (DES) and alpha-B-crystallin (CRYAB) among the classic causes, alongside myotilin, ZASP, filamin C and others
Respiratory muscle weakness and peripheral neuropathy may accompany the myopathy
Muscle biopsy shows Z-disc streaming, rimmed vacuoles and aggregates of desmin and other proteins on immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy
Because cardiac and respiratory complications drive morbidity, systematic cardiac and respiratory surveillance is central to management
reference.pathophysiology: Myofibrillar myopathies are caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins of the sarcomeric Z-disc and its associated cytoskeletal network, including desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, myotilin, ZASP and filamin C. These proteins maintain the structural integrity and mechanical linkage of the myofibrils and the intermediate-filament scaffold that connects sarcomeres to the sarcolemma and organelles. When they are defective, the Z-disc disintegrates and misfolded proteins, particularly desmin, accumulate as insoluble aggregates that disrupt myofibrillar architecture, mitochondrial positioning and protein-quality-control pathways. The resulting mechanical and metabolic failure of the fibre produces progressive weakness, and because several of these proteins are also essential in cardiac muscle, cardiomyopathy and conduction disease are frequent.
additionalDifferentials: Distal myopathies including GNE and Miyoshi myopathy
Chronic inflammatory or hereditary neuropathies where neuropathy coexists
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, which is often normal to moderately elevated
Electromyography, which may show myopathic changes sometimes with myotonic or neurogenic features
Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy showing protein aggregates and Z-disc pathology
Cardiac assessment with electrocardiogram, echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
Targeted or panel genetic testing covering desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, myotilin, ZASP, filamin C and related genes
redFlags: Cardiac conduction block, arrhythmia or heart failure, which can be life-threatening and may precede weakness
Respiratory muscle weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation
Rapid functional decline suggesting an aggressive subtype
Sudden cardiac events in the patient or affected relatives
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with the causative gene, but progression is usually slow for the skeletal weakness while cardiac and respiratory complications are the main determinants of morbidity and mortality, so outcomes are substantially improved by early detection and treatment of heart and respiratory involvement.
pitfalls: Focusing on the skeletal weakness and failing to screen for the potentially fatal cardiac disease
Mislabelling it as a limb-girdle dystrophy and missing the diagnostic aggregate pathology
Overlooking coexisting peripheral neuropathy or respiratory involvement
Assuming a single gene, when the group is genetically heterogeneous and needs broad testing
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Undertake cardiac surveillance with electrocardiography, echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, treating conduction disease and considering a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator to prevent sudden death
Monitor respiratory function and institute non-invasive ventilation for respiratory muscle weakness
Maintain mobility and function with physiotherapy, orthoses such as ankle-foot orthoses and occupational therapy
Manage dysphagia and nutrition with speech and language therapy and dietetic support
Confirm the causative gene, such as desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, myotilin, ZASP or filamin C, by genetic testing to refine surveillance
Offer genetic counselling and cardiac screening of at-risk relatives
Coordinate care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
